news.n_title: Public services commission exams, gig workers' plight next on CJP agenda: Abhijeet Dipke
news.n_description: An exclusive conversation with the Cockroach Janata Party founder on the outfit's plans, joining politics, the Centre's exam reforms and the Jantar Mantar protest

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
After securing the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as the Union education minister over the NEET-UG paper leak, the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has trained its guns on alleged irregularities in public services commission exams in various states. The outfit says it will also focus on issues faced by unorganised sector labour, such as gig workers on food delivery platforms.

In a conversation with INDIA TODAY at his home in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (formerly Aurangabad) in Maharashtra, CJP founder and convenor Abhijeet Dipke said that the CJP protest at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar drew support not just from NEET aspirants but also young Indians disillusioned over alleged irregularities in public services commission examinations.

“The reason we are going to Bihar is that most of the crowd at Jantar Mantar was from Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh. The youth in these states are dependent on public services [commission exams] for their social upliftment,” said Dipke.

“These students are very frustrated. They asked us why we were speaking only about NEET and not the public services commission exams. This is a massive concern across India,” he added, stating that complaints about irregularities in public services commission exams and government recruitments had come from across states.

The CJP has announced a pan-India public outreach, ‘Kya Bolti Public’, to expand its footprint. It will involve visiting states to hear out aggrieved citizens. Dipke said the aim was to “revive the culture of public listening”, and that the CJP movement itself was born out of the culture of listening to the people.

Dipke said students from Bihar had invited the CJP to their state to address concerns around public services exams. He added that the norms for recruitment by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) had been changed around 2012, leading to higher intake of aspirants from science, mathematics and English language backgrounds. This has inconvenienced those from humanities and vernacular language education. Those preparing for UPSC examinations at coaching centres battled lodging challenges too, having to stay in dingy rooms in cities and facing harassment from landlords.

The CJP, Dipke said, would also take up the welfare of gig workers, given the heavy presence of food delivery platform workers at Jantar Mantar. “The concept of gig working is good for western countries as the society is uplifted; in India, gig working is nothing but exploitation of labour. They need a major policy reform, a safety net... They are forced to put their lives at risk for a small incentive,” he said.

Asked about the CJP’s long -term goal, Dipke said: “We want to change the political discourse.” Youth-centric issues remain the focus. “Empathy and compassion are on the decline in society. We have started becoming sadists,” he added, noting that some people had even started drawing pleasure from seeing others in trouble.

“Ours used to be an aspirational society,” said Dipke, pointing out that movements like India Against Corruption were meant to create a better nation. “That India wanted to move forward. Today’s India is just happy it is surviving. Now, citizens aren’t much aspirational,” he said, reasoning that this conditioning was pushing India behind by decades.

Abhijeet Dipke spoke at length to INDIA TODAY on the issues at hand, how the party intends to reform education and the achievements at Jantar Mantar. Excerpts:

Q. What are the CJP’s plans going ahead?
A. The issue of unemployment looms before us. The crowd at Jantar Mantar was not just made up of students, but also those from the 25- to 35- year age group. Many protesters had degrees, but lacked jobs. Most people at Jantar Mantar were from Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Uttar Pradesh, as the youth there are dependent on the Public Services Commission (PSC) exams for social upliftment. These students are very frustrated. They asked us why we were speaking only about NEET and not the PSC exams. Complaints about irregularities in these exams and government recruitments have come from states across India. There is anger over the quality of education and its unaffordability too.

The CJP will also take up issues related to gig workers. A large number of Swiggy and Zomato workers turned up at the protest. The concept of gig working is good for western countries; in India, gig working is nothing but exploitation of labour. They need a safety net. We will also focus on complaints over E20 blended petrol. First, we will go to every state and district, hold public meetings and understand people’s concerns and expectations from us. While interacting with the youth at Jantar Mantar, I realised that they are not taken seriously and are dismissed as a non-serious generation. They cannot be dismissed because their style of communication and lifestyle are different.

Q. Does the CJP have political plans?
A. If the people want us to, we will have to consider it, but we have no such plans as of now. The CJP is a social movement. People have lost faith in all institutions. Public representatives change loyalties soon after being elected. The courts side with the ruling party and people are upset at the Enforcement Directorate (ED), Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and even the media. India needs a social movement in which people can rise above political affiliations. If we convert the CJP into a political outfit, they may unleash the ED or CBI on us.

Q. What do you have to say about the charges that Left parties were spearheading the protest?
A. Student organisations across parties were involved—the National Students Union of India (NSUI), Association of Students for Alternative Politics (ASAP) of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and those from the Left. Leftist groups are being highlighted intentionally—all Opposition parties like the Congress, DMK, Trinamool Congress, Samajwadi Party, Shiv Sena (UBT), NCP and AAP supported us.

Q. What about the alleged violence by protesters at Jantar Mantar?
A. Outsiders had infiltrated the protest. Officers and constables from the Delhi Police who sympathised with our cause told us that this was being done to serve as a justification for a crackdown. On July 19, a truck loaded with stones was parked, along with a broken-down van, by Delhi Police to serve as evidence of stone pelting by CJP supporters. The police claimed that 2,100 criminals were at Jantar Mantar. We were frisked while entering; why wasn’t this done for them? This was pre-planned.

Q. How do you see Sonam Wangchuk’s move to withdraw his fast?
A. We always told Sonam Sir to break his fast while we continued with our agitation. We were happy and relieved when he broke his fast. He was almost kidnapped from Jantar Mantar. Our team was not allowed to meet him. We couldn’t communicate with him.

Q. What education reforms does the CJP want to introduce?
A. Primary schooling must improve. In the last decade, around 94,000 government-run schools have shut down, which means this was meant to benefit private schools. In the US, I did not see a single coaching class. Here, a nexus between the coaching industry and private schools/ colleges is obvious.

Q. What do you think about the Union government’s Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026?
A. We are not satisfied. The focus is on what is to be done after a paper leak, which means the government takes a leak for granted. The focus must be on preventing it. Our demand for Rs 1 crore compensation for the kin of students who have died by suicide stands. The government says it will have to check rules before announcing it. The same regime cocks a snook at rules when it pays MPs/ MLAs crores for destabilising governments. We will agitate again if this is not met.

Q. What’s the biggest takeaway from the CJP protest?
A. The biggest, most significant, achievement was that repressed voices overcame their fear and found the courage to express themselves and started questioning the central government.

news.n_title: From the India Today archives (1983) | Phoolan Devi: End of the trail
news.n_description: August 10 is Phoolan Devi's birthday. The surrender saga of one of India's most-infamous dacoits

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
(NOTE: This article was originally published in the India Today issue dated February 28, 1983)

The whole sequence had a touch of the charade, as if a carefully-planned rehearsal had gone awry on the opening day. When the curtain finally went up on the surrender of Phoolan Devi and 25 other dacoits in Bhind, a district headquarters about 75 km from Gwalior last week, many pieces of the jigsaw leading to the momentous event remained missing. And as many myths about the queen of criminal violence, whose reported exploits had mesmerised the public mind, for over two years lay shattered in the dust.

After the vigorous media build-up she had been accorded, Phoolan Devi, the dramatic centre of Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Arjun Singh’s extravagant public relations exercise, turned out to be the chief disappointment. She was neither nebulous nor nubile, as countless reporters and writers including the illustrious Khushwant Singh who went on her trail last year, had imagined her. Nor was she malevolently dangerous - no more or less, that is, than any other sizeable dacoit gang - as she had been made out to be. Worst, it became certain that she is not the only woman dacoit in existence, and it is yet to be established that she was a gang leader supreme - in fact, it was clearly understood that she operated only in close collusion with her present lover Man Singh or other lovers in the past who remained de facto leaders and organisers.

ANTI-CLIMAX: Instead, the "daredevil dacoit queen", the "black beauty of the bandit world" or the dasyu sundari (dacoit beauty) known to sport bell-bottom trousers and bobbed hair, turned out to be a drab-looking, highly moody, childishly petulant, and disastrously short-tempered girl on a rampage. There was little about her to suggest the high-minded and seductive woman out to avenge her honour and redeem the humiliations of a tormented past. Even the police officer responsible for negotiating the terms of her surrender.

Rajendra Chaturvedi, superintendent of police (SP) of Bhind district,described her as "brash, hasty, immature and short-tempered," saying that, "it was the press who blew her image totally out of proportion." The gradually built-up myth that has grown about a woman defending her honour is as fake as the tales of her sensational looks; the impression of her as an original, innovative, wildly daring and fearsome victor in life is nothing but a cover-up, more likely than not, for a neurotic, highly-strung, evil-tempered and foulmouthed victim of life, a casualty whose life has been made more bleak by the clout and celebrity her offences have brought her.

Says M.D. Sharma, Deputy Inspector General. (Chambal range) of the Phoolan Devi phenomenon: "Most people in cities imagine that drop-outs from society- are an urban, middle class feature. They’re not. Phoolan is a classic example of a rural drop-out who took a lot of persuasion to be brought back to her senses."

UNLIKELY BANDIT: It is hard to believe looking her slight short figure - she is under five ft in height and her ravaged face - that this is the woman who terrorised large sections of the population in two states. It is hard to imagine this scruffy, edgy, nervous girl as someone who toted a gun - her wrists seem too painfully thin to even carry one around.

As she sits huddled in the fold of her family - three sisters, a brother, old mother and father - and her gang, it is impossible to believe that this sad, wasted creature was capable of a large-scale butchery, countless kidnappings, and deliberate instances of cold-blooded murder. Almost the only time her eyes light up and her face breaks into a smile is when she is cuddling children; at all other times she retreats into sullen silence or erupts snarling and mouthing foul abuse.

But Phoolan Devi, the prized product of mostly media fantasy and some cold-blooded fact, didn’t take long to become a vital prestige issue - an issue that set two state police services at war and a calculating chief minister at extracting the maximum populist benefit.

Phoolan’s surrender - according to senior Madhya Pradesh police officials involved it has been imminent since last summer - was kept a closely-guarded state Government secret, then slowly publicised (every section of the national press had been forewarned at least 24 hours in advance) and finally mounted as a spectacular public show. Sadly, the whole exercise flopped.

Two days before Phoolan’s surrender took place at the Parade Ground in Bhind, she was housed in a distant Irrigation Department bungalow together with her lover Man Singh, her entire family and her gang. For three days before she actually surrendered on February 12, the Madhya Pradesh police had been announcing her surrender, which was postponed thrice. Not only because Phoolan wanted her family beside her before the event but equally because a nasty row erupted between Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh police officials.

POLICE RIVALRY: On January 6, when Madhya Pradesh police officials quietly brought over Phoolan’s family from their village Sheikhpur Guda in Uttar Pradesh’s Jalaun district to Bhind, the Uttar Pradesh police registered a case of kidnapping against the SP of Bhind and accompanying policemen. A day later when another contingent went over to bring Man Singh’s family, the Uttar Pradesh police simply arrested the six policemen of Bhind district including a sub-inspector.

The Uttar Pradesh police force’s pique at having the thunder of Phoolan’s farewell to arms stolen from them was so great, that acrimonious accusations were exchanged at the highest level. In fact, the rivalry to acquire Phoolan had become so embittered that a Madhya Pradesh policeman despatched to "kidnap" Man Singh’s family even fired at the Uttar Pradesh police giving them chase.

MEDIATION EFFORTS: First attempts towards getting Phoolan to surrender were made in early July 1982. Informers were of little help. Malkhan Singh, released on parole in November, dilly-dallied as another surrender soon after his would have taken the limelight from him. Ghanshyam’s relations with Malkhan were strained and he refused to accept his mediation.

After Ghanshyam’s attempt to surrender to the Uttar Pradesh police at Rampura in Jalaun district on November 18 failed, he approached Chaturvedi and they finally met on December 20, Muslim, another dacoit who had received feelers for his and Phoolan’s surrender - they had once been together - also got in touch with Chaturvedi. By early January, Muslim and his men had moved into the Umri police circle while Phoolan with her gang was in the Nayagaon area. It was understood that they would be left alone during negotiations.

To thwart any attempt by the furious Uttar Pradesh police on the dacoits’ life, security on the border was tightened, and at 12 points along the boundary, pickets were posted to keep an eye on the neighbouring police - especially the Provincial Armed Constabulary - who made forays into Madhya Pradesh.

There was disagreement between Madhya Pradesh policemen, too. On January 26, a police party appeared abruptly in the Umri area and fired at Muslim and his men. The dacoit leader was shot in the abdomen but dragged himself for 10 km and went into hiding, from where he sent Chaturvedi a message. The alarmed Chaturvedi arranged for Muslim’s treatment first in Bhind and later in Gwalior, where he is now recovering in police custody.

PRECIPITOUS STEPS: A panicky Phoolan fled with her gang soon after the encounter; so did Ghanshyam, hiding in Datia district near Seondha. As far as they knew, they had been betrayed. By this time an order from Bhopal said that the surrender must take place - if at all - by February 10 since it had taken too long already. Chaturvedi, playing dangerously, went unarmed and alone into the ravines looking for Ghanshyam and Phoolan to lure them back. He succeeded but only after convincing them that the policemen had shot at Muslim accidentally.

Similarly, on February 6, the Madhya Pradesh police suddenly started combing operations in the Seondha dang (forest) in Datia district knowing full well that the Ghanshyam gang was there waiting for the surrender. Ghanshyam could well have been killed that day except that Bhopal got to know about the operation and angrily ordered that it be suspended immediately. The orders were reportedly issued from the chief minister’s secretariat.

Once, however, Phoolan became Madhya Pradesh police’s property, the chief minister swung into action to put up the most effective show for her surrender. Early morning on February 12, he appeared on the roof of the local school at Bhind to receive homage from the gathered dacoits.

Although the press - domestic and international - had turned out in full force thanks to publicity of the Madhya Pradesh police and public relations department, the audience in the grounds below was no more than a crowd of about 4,000, a sad come down from the 30,000 who had congregated in the same ground last summer to witness the surrender of dacoit Malkhan Singh.

No sooner had the ceremony started, with the dacoits lining up to shed their weapons and cartridge belts before portraits of Mahatma Gandhi and the Durga Mata, and garlanding the chief minister, a few members of the audience began to shout slogans and shout abuse at the chief minister. One of them tried to throw a stone, while screaming at the top his voice: "Goli ke badle goli. Daku ko hero banate ho. Churiyan pehan ke behto." (A Bullet for a bullet. You are making heroes of dacoits. Why don’t you wear bangles and sit at home.)

Quickly pounced upon by policemen he had to be carried out, and the crowd grew restive. In fact, it was the barrage of cameramen blocking the crowd’s view of the dacoits that disturbed and scattered the audience, even as the chief minister smugly basked in the enormous publicity the spectacle would bring him.

PERFECT IRONY: It was the perfect irony, of course, that the dacoits, even at the moment of their social rehabilitation were being exploited just as they had been at the outset of their terrorist careers to seek an alternate existence as desperadoes outside the social system. For much as the romanticised media reports have us believe, the act of their daring the truth is quite the reverse: any policeman connected in an anti-dacoit effort will concede that being a dacoit is one of the hardest, meanest ways of living.

And, that most dacoits offer to surrender, because they are played out by the sheer physical hardship of their existence. Moving under cover, like guerillas, from forest to forest, ravine to ravine, going without food for days, organising and reorganising themselves, while constantly being pursued by the police in encounters, they are the worst survivors of all.

Dacoit Karan Singh, elder brother of the ferocious Ghanshyam Singh who also surrendered last week, is a tall whiskered man in an Uttar Pradesh policeman’s uniform. One of a gang of eight, which also included Phoolan in the past, he remembers taking to the ravines in 1974. The local priest in his village had, in collusion with the patwari, acquired his family’s rightful property. In revenge, he and Ghanshyam killed the priest.

The path to other dacoities, kidnappings, murders-a total of 56 offences today and an award of Rs 7,000 by the Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh governments on his head-followed. Both brothers were once in Malkhan Singh’s gang; when Malkhan gave up last year, they carried on.

Easily one of the most powerful dacoit gangs operating in the region, armed with self-loading rifles that make Phoolan’s Mausers and 12-bore rifles look like toys, Ghanshyam and Karan Singh have clear memories of the nearly 10 years they spent as dacoits. Ghanshyam, also known as Baba, remembers going without any food for up to four days frequently.

Karan Singh, married unlike his brother, only recalls being able to visit his family once in all those years. Says the long-haired, bearded, vicious-looking Ghanshyam: "We had enough of it. Enough of that life. Now that our enmity is avenged we can live like normal human beings."

Munni Bai, a dark, strikingly-featured, pockmarked woman dacoit with her husband Babu Khan has been part of Ghanshyam’s gang since 1977; both husband and wife who lived in a village in Bhind district, quit after they had been accused by the panchayat of committing a murder. Fleeing into the forest they met up with Ghanshyam and took to the itinerant life of the marauder.

"It was our circumstances that led us to it," she says, "for five years we had no home, the only objects of worship we knew were our weapons. Now even if we are in jail, we can do what we like. We will not always be on the run."

Almost every dacoit claims a similar history: of being falsely accused in a crime. Almost all dacoits claim motivation for turning into dacoits from the same source: to wreak vengeance on those who once victimised them.

SURVIVAL: Once they embarked upon the course, it was generally the pressure of survival that egged them on beside the clout they gathered by successfully terrorising villages under their control, and the money earned through demanding ransoms in kidnapping cases. Significantly, most of the dacoits who surrendered in Bhind last week brought sizeable sums of cash with them, varying between Rs 20,000 and Rs 40,000, sewn into pouches lined inside their clothes.

In Phoolan Devi’s case, the original motivation to turn to violence seems to be abetted by another factor: sex. Most newspapers keep primly referring to her series of lovers - the present one is Man Singh - as "paramour", as if she were some kind of Madame Bovary of the Chambal ravines. Few seem to make the simple connection between her early rejection by husband and family and the drift into promiscuity. Daughter of impoverished parents, she was thrown out by her husband who was nearly 20 years older soon after she married him, at the age of 13.

Unacceptable in her parents’ home when she returned, and accused of committing a dacoity by her uncle, she emerged from a spell in jail to forge a relationship with Vikram who initiated her into the trade. Slipping into the underworld of hardened criminals, she began to crack up after Vikram was killed in 1980. Putting her act together the only way she knew, she tried to seek out Sri Ram and Lala Ram, two men who she suspected as being responsible for his murder.

It was while pursuing them that she was led to commit the brutal massacre of 20 Thakurs in Behmai village in Kanpur district. Both the men she sought to kill in revenge were not in Behmai that fateful day, but the atrocity that she conducted with her then lover-accomplice, Mustaqueem. created a fear psychosis among Thakurs and contributed to her legend.

Since then, she has drifted around, skilfully evading the police, once rumoured to have escaped to Nepal where the Government reportedly placed an award of Rs 1 lakh upon her head, and ganging up with Man Singh with whom she has remained since. Their 66 crimes, of dacoity, kidnapping, instances of murder, attempted murder and dacoity with murder, have invested them, and her in particular, with a bizarre kind of glamour, as epitomised by Hollywood stereotypes like Bonnie and Clyde.

DECLINING NUMBERS: She is not the only one. There is more than one female dacoit still at large, among them Kusuma Nain and Geeta Thakur, though Madhya Pradesh police officials claim that the number of dacoits in their state has dropped dramatically in the last two years-from about 500 in 1980-81 to about 30 at present.

At least 160 have been killed in encounters with the police, while the rest are serving jail sentences. The state police has, however, only lost one head constable in encounters since 1980 when the anti-dacoity campaign was intensified in the six districts of Guna, Shivpuri, Datia, Gwalior, Bhind and Morena.

Phoolan Devi who, so far, has had her demands for surrendering acceded (she insisted that her family as well as her cow and goat to be transferred to her in Madhya Pradesh) has at least 14 more before proceeding to Gwalior jail. Among them: that she shall not be hanged, that she shall be kept in an open jail and not be handcuffed, be given A Class treatment and tried in a special court, that all cases against her will be transferred from Uttar Pradesh to Madhya Pradesh, that safety assurances be provided for her family, along with land for them and a job for her brother. All this, she says defiantly, should be accompanied with a signed message from Rajiv Gandhi.

If Phoolan was reluctant to be photographed until the actual surrender, it was because she was under the impression that her "every picture was worth a lakh ruppes". She couldn’t get that out of her mind and was furious that she was obviously being cheated out of millions of rupees by news photographers.

All this did not seem very funny early on the morning of the surrender when Phoolan started throwing tantrums and threatened to walk out if she was not given her rightful share of the money that news photographers were making off her. The situation was getting out of hand until Ghanshyam, tired of her eccentricities and her histrionics, half threatened, half bullied her back into the fold.

"She may demand anything," admits a police official, "but she will be tried through a proper legal process; only she will be guaranteed a basically human treatment." It is estimated that with the trail of crime behind her, she will spend a minimum of ten years in jail. But her strange and fascinating saga will remain alive, for no other reason, than as a reflection of the primitive and contemporary colliding in human nature and Indian society.

news.n_title: Why Sambhal violence report is the new BJP-SP flashpoint before UP polls
news.n_description: The report, which blames Samajwadi Party leaders, comes handy for the BJP to claim that law and order is a casualty wherever its political rival is influential

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Cornered over the Ayodhya Ram Temple donation pilferage and ethanol-blended petrol rows and lately the student protests for examination reforms, the BJP in Uttar Pradesh may have found a counter-pain point of the Opposition Samajwadi Party (SP)—the November 2024 violence in Sambhal over a court-mandated survey of the Shahi Jama Masjid located in Chandausi town.

A judicial commission's report, tabled in the legislative assembly on August 5, has concluded that the violence was “pre-planned”, given the police a clean chit and pointed towards the alleged role of SP MP Zia-ur-Rehman Barq, party MLA Iqbal Mahmood’s son Suhail Iqbal and others in the law and order breakdown.

The report has handed the BJP fresh ammunition against the SP in the run-up to the UP assembly elections due early next year.

The 854-page report was prepared by a commission headed by retired Allahabad High Court judge Justice Devendra Arora, with former IPS officer A.K. Jain and former IAS officer Amit Prasad as the other members. The commission was constituted by the Yogi Adityanath government.

The violence in Sambhal erupted when officials arrived to conduct the second phase of a survey ordered by a local court on a petition that claimed that the 16th-century mosque was built over a Hindu temple. Clashes between protesters and the police, arson, stone-pelting and firing were reported. Four people were killed while several others, including police personnel, were injured.

The commission concluded that the violence was not a spontaneous public reaction but a planned act. According to the report, preparations for the unrest began immediately after the first survey on November 19, when the exercise remained incomplete but passed off peacefully.

The report states that misinformation was spread among Muslims that the survey was a plot to seize or demolish the mosque. In reality, the commission observed, the court had only directed an assessment relating to maintenance and public access of the mosque under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958. The misinformation created fear and resentment, helping mobilise a crowd before the second survey, the report states.

The commission significantly concluded that the bullets that killed people were not fired from police weapons. It also noted that 28 police personnel were injured during the violence, including seven with bullet injuries. According to the report, members of the crowd attempted to snatch police weapons, attacked government personnel and damaged public property. The district administration and the police gave a restrained and appropriate response.

The political ramifications of the report are expected to be significant. The BJP has built one of its strongest electoral narratives in UP around improved law and order under chief minister Adityanath. The party has repeatedly contrasted its governance with what it describes as the “goonda raj” of previous SP regimes. The administration’s bulldozer action against alleged criminals, claims of riot-free governance and tough policing have remained central themes of the BJP's campaign in past elections.

The Sambhal probe report now gives the BJP an official judicial document to reinforce that narrative. The findings relating to alleged involvement of SP leaders fit into the BJP’s argument that law and order deteriorated whenever the SP was in power or influential locally.

Not that the SP will accept the report quietly. The party is expected to question its conclusions and project it as a politically motivated exercise in the run-up to elections. Much like it has challenged investigations into other politically sensitive cases, the SP is likely to argue that the report selectively targets Opposition leaders while absolving the administration.

“The report is one-sided and appears designed to place the entire blame on one community. When the chief minister himself speaks in terms of 80 versus 20, it is difficult to expect an impartial investigation from such a government. This is unfortunate,” SP spokesperson Manoj Singh Kaka said.

“There is already material on record showing that some police officials in Sambhal had political links and were working for the BJP while in uniform. The people of Sambhal have neither accepted communalism nor participated in it,” he emphasised.

However, BJP spokesperson Rakesh Tripathi said the report was prepared only after examining all the evidence in detail. “These findings are based on a thorough investigation and are backed by evidence. The report clearly shows the involvement of SP leaders and how they attempted to incite violence. Their objective was to use Sambhal to destabilise the Yogi Adityanath government and trigger wider unrest across western UP. However, the local administration acted in time and foiled those attempts,” he said.

The political contest comes at a crucial juncture since both the BJP and the Opposition have been broadening their campaign themes. The SP and Congress have questioned the BJP over governance issues and accountability. But the BJP now appears to have an opportunity to shift the narrative back to law and order, communal violence and public security.

The Sambhal report also places the violence within the city's longer communal history, noting that repeated communal tensions in the district over the years have deepened social divisions. That broader historical context may also find place in the BJP's campaign as it argues for firm governance under its umbrella.

With the report tabled in the legislative assembly, expect it to become a major political issue in the run-up to the 2027 elections, and both the BJP and SP reinforcing sharply different narratives on governance, law and order and communal harmony.

news.n_title: The Gen Z reset: Mohan Bhagwat's model and the stakes it raises for BJP
news.n_description: The RSS chief has said Gen Z anger is real and its protest legitimate. For the BJP and Modi regime, it means a reconnect with young Indians earned through outcomes

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) does not do U-turns. It drifts instead. A word is swapped here, a platform chosen there, an emphasis moved so slowly that you notice it only in hindsight. That is why Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat’s recent run of speeches to young Indians, the Gen Z, is worth reading closely, and also why the venue of the last address mattered nearly as much as its script.

On August 6, at the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre in Mumbai, and before more than 2,000 students drawn from over a hundred cities for the 15th anniversary conference of India’s International Movement to Unite Nations (IIMUM), Bhagwat said something RSS sarsanghchalaks are not often heard saying. “If you ask me to trust blindly, I’ll trust Gen Z,” he stated, calling this generation more honest than his own.

Bhagwat was equally direct on the accusation that the recent crop of young protesters was working against the interests of the country. If Gen Z is agitating, he said, they “certainly aren’t anti-nationals”. What they wanted, in his account, was to be taken seriously rather than managed. “They should be heard and felt heard,” he said.

Protest itself Bhagwat treated as ordinary democratic business rather than a threat. “Protest is also a way of dialogue,” he said, describing agitation as what follows when concerns go unheard through other channels. He attached one condition, which was that the purpose of it all should be to build consensus rather than to create divisions.

The venue deserves as much attention as the remarks. Bhagwat did not choose a Sangh shibir or an Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) convention. IIMUN is a model UN organisation that draws school and college students of no fixed ideological address, and it has at different times put Narendra Modi and Rahul Gandhi on the same stage. This was an aspirational, urban and heavily online audience that every party in the country is currently trying to read.

Bhagwat’s speech closed a sequence that ran through the previous fortnight. In Delhi on July 25, at the concluding session of the Vishwamangalya Sabha’s meeting on contemporary motherhood, he had set out the narrative shift in plain domestic terms. “When we were young, it was an era of obedience,” he said. “The new generation asks questions. We have to explain the reasoning to them.” What was required now, he added, was “not dictation, but discussion”.

Two days later in Hyderabad, he turned to the generation itself, and the tone changed. Gen Z was adaptable, emotional by nature and quickly drawn to whatever struck it as visibly authentic. “They do not think with a very calm mind,” he said. He offered this as observation. A fair number of listeners heard condescension.

Put the three speeches together and the arc becomes legible. The first acknowledged that the old transmission belt of authority had snapped. The second attempted to explain the people at the far end of it. The third, in Mumbai, conceded that they might actually have a point.

The timing is not mysterious. Indian politics has spent months absorbing student anger over the NEET (national medical entrance) paper leak, the examination system coming under a cloud, recruitment that stalls for years, and jobs that never quite arrive. Much of that anger has come from first-time voters and the enormous population of aspirants grinding through competitive examinations. This is a cohort that grades governments on delivery, and it says so publicly and quickly, and on platforms where a narrative can turn over in an afternoon.

The BJP has been adjusting to that for some time. Prime Minister Modi has promised fast-track courts for paper leak cases and a broader clean-up of the examination system, and in parallel the party has rebuilt its outreach around softer formats, such as podcasts, unstructured interviews and social media conversations, with Modi himself doing much of the work.

Bhagwat’s intervention sits inside that same effort rather than apart from it, even though he is not speaking for the government and is announcing no policy. His role, as it has always been, is to set the mood within the Sangh ecosystem. Telling that ecosystem that Gen Z’s frustrations are genuine amounts to an instruction to engage rather than dismiss.

What Bhagwat left out is at least as revealing. He endorsed no particular protest. He criticised no minister and no ministry. He did not point at any institution or hold it responsible for youth discontent. He warned instead against believing what circulates online without verifying it, and argued for self-imposed discipline rather than bans. And he drew a distinction between protest that strengthens democracy and protest that corrodes it, and between grievance aimed at reform and grievance aimed at confrontation. That is recognisably the old Sangh preference for social cohesion, restated for a generation that will not sit through a lecture.

There is a recent precedent for the mistake Bhagwat seems determined to avoid, and it is not a comfortable one for the Sangh. When central farm laws brought hundreds of thousands of protesters to the borders of Delhi in the winter of 2020, the ecosystem around the government reached for the shortest available explanation. The protesters were Khalistani or fronting for them. They were professional agitators and foreign funded. The label moved fast through television studios and WhatsApp groups, and then it did something nobody using it had planned for. It stopped landing on the protesters and began landing on the constituency behind them.

A farmer in Sangrur or Muzaffarnagar who had never been near a dharna heard himself described as a separatist on prime time. By the time the ruling ecosystem tried to construct a counter-narrative, there was no clean surface left to build one on. The laws were repealed in November 2021. The resentment stayed a good deal longer.

Almost every line of Bhagwat’s Mumbai speech was engineered to prevent a repeat. The young protester was kept inside the national family as our own people, the next generation. They are not anti-national. The Sangh’s most dependable rhetorical instrument, the boundary between us and them, was deliberately holstered, and its use against the young was ruled out of order before anyone reached for it. The lesson of 2021 had been applied.

The analogy only carries the BJP so far, though. Farmers were a constituency with an address. They had unions, spokespersons, a negotiating committee and a single reversible demand, and the government could repeal three laws and end the agitation in a day, however humiliating the retreat be. Gen Z offers none of that. There is arguably nobody to summon for talks, no charter to concede and no signature that repairs a broken recruitment cycle. Declining to call them anti-national removes an insult. It does not supply a remedy.

It is also worth noticing where this discipline is being applied and where not. The delegitimising label was eventually retired for farmers and is being retired in advance for students—and both are constituencies the party needs and still largely holds onto. The Sangh has learned that branding a whole generation disloyal is a self-inflicted wound. It has also learned not to fall in the trap of social media campaigns from fringes and groups with vested interests. It has learned only to be careful about which groups it aims the brand at. The test will not be what Bhagwat says from a stage in Mumbai. It will be what a BJP spokesman says on television on a bad news night, and whether anyone in the ecosystem is corrected when the old reflex returns.

For the BJP, however, Gen Z sympathy raises the stakes. Once the ideological parent has said in public that the young are right to be angry, the political wing loses the easy option of arguing that they have been misled. Empathy is a cheque the government now has to cash, and it will be cashed in examination calendars that hold, recruitment boards that finish what they start, and results that arrive when they were promised. Young voters are not going to accept tone in lieu of outcomes.

That is the deeper construct. Political loyalty used to be inherited from a family, a caste, a neighbourhood or a union. This generation rents its allegiance rather than inheriting it. It rewards whoever is performing, it switches without much guilt, and it is far less anchored by ideological identity than the voters who came before. It is also the first cohort to experience politics almost entirely in real time, where credibility is retested every few hours and yesterday’s goodwill is not carried forward.

For a BJP that has spent a decade cultivating a young and dynamic image, that is uncomfortable arithmetic. Reconnecting will take more than another round of digital campaigning. It will require rebuilding trust in the institutions that actually shape a 22-year-old’s life, among them the examination body, the recruitment board, the university and the employment office.

For the RSS, whose influence has always rested on slow social work rather than election cycles, Bhagwat’s speeches suggest a translation exercise in which the same worldview is rendered into a language Gen Z will sit through. The claim is not that authority no longer matters. It is that authority must now be earned in conversation instead of assumed by seniority.

Whether this is tactical repositioning or something more durable will take years to establish. What is already clear is that the Sangh has registered the shift and has stopped talking at the young in favour of talking to them. The harder part is not his to deliver. Bhagwat can open a conversation, but he cannot fill a vacancy or clean up an examination. Whether any of this converts into political trust will be settled somewhere far less rhetorical, in the recruitment lists, the results calendars and the job numbers that made the conversation necessary in the first place.
