news.n_title: Mojtaba remains out of public eye, Iran promises new footage of Supreme Leader
news.n_description: The announcement comes as questions persist over Khamenei's limited public appearances since he succeeded his father, Ali Khamenei, as Iran's supreme leader in March.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Iranian authorities have signalled that new footage of Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei will be released in the future, amid continued speculation about his health and prolonged absence from public view.

The development comes after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met Khamenei in late July, according to state media. The meeting, held around the start of Pezeshkian’s third year in office, reportedly focused on military affairs and key economic issues, including foreign exchange management, energy consumption and economic ties with international partners.

Adding to the focus on Khamenei's public profile, Basij Organisation deputy Qasem Qoraishi said footage and other material showing the Supreme Leader among the public, on the streets and in meetings with armed forces commanders would be released in the future. He said the material would help counter criticism and speculation surrounding Khamenei's condition.

The announcement comes as questions persist over Khamenei’s limited public appearances since he succeeded his father, Ali Khamenei, as Iran’s supreme leader in March.

Days after Israeli media reports claimed that Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei was in an “extremely critical condition”, Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency released an undated video on August 9 showing him interacting with followers and appearing to be in good health. The footage appeared aimed at countering speculation about his condition.

CONTRADICTORY SIGNALS ON ACCESS

President Pezeshkian has offered differing accounts in recent weeks about his interactions with Khamenei. On July 21, he said his engagements with the supreme leader were increasing steadily. However, in early August, he described communication with Khamenei as "very difficult", fuelling further speculation about the leader’s accessibility.

State media reported that the late-July meeting between the two leaders covered a range of strategic issues, including military matters, resource management and efforts to strengthen Iran’s economic partnerships abroad.

KHAMENEI YET TO APPEAR IN PUBLIC AFTER ASSUMING OFFICE

Khamenei has largely remained out of public view since assuming the country’s highest office following the death of his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, in a February 28 strike during the US-Israel war on Iran.

Reports at the time suggested that Mojtaba Khamenei was also seriously injured in the attack. Even before becoming supreme leader, he maintained a relatively low public profile compared with other senior Iranian officials.

In May, Iranian state media reported what it described as the first publicly acknowledged meeting between Pezeshkian and Khamenei since the leadership transition. The two were said to have held several hours of discussions.

The planned release of new images and footage is likely to be closely watched as Iranian authorities seek to dispel rumours surrounding the supreme leader’s health and demonstrate his continued involvement in state affairs.

news.n_title: Sports Minister says Indian football is making excellent progress. But where?
news.n_description: Indian football is desperate for stability, yet the Sports Minister sees "excellent progress". Between club exits, financial uncertainty, falling broadcast value and national-team confusion, the reality looks very different.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
“Football is making excellent progress.”

If you are an Indian football fan reading that line, there is a fair chance you are wondering whether you have just walked into some elaborate ragebait. It is, in fact, a comment made by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya while speaking about Indian football on the sidelines of the 85th edition of Fit India Sundays on Cycle.

And yes, he was talking about the same Indian football ecosystem currently trying to make sense of club exits, financial uncertainty, a changing ISL structure and a national-team setup that has had its own share of confusion.

#WATCH | Hanol Village, Gujarat: On the 85th edition of Fit India: Sundays On Cycle, Union Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya says, “I am delighted that the initiative has evolved into a major movement to advance the Prime Minister's Fit India Movement. Young people across more pic.twitter.com/RkdmM5uAv6

— ANI (@ANI) August 9, 2026

The Indian Super League will return, as Mandaviya said, but the bigger picture around Indian football remains far more difficult than that one fact suggests.

After the uncertainty around the competition last season, having a league back on the calendar matters for clubs, players and supporters. But the return of the competition cannot by itself be treated as proof that Indian football is in good health, or making "excellent progress"

That is certainly setting the bar at a historic low.

While the ISL is finding a way back, clubs are struggling to make the numbers work, investors are stepping away and the commercial structure of the league is still being rebuilt.

The latest blow came when Tata Steel decided to withdraw Jamshedpur FC from the ISL for the 2026-27 season. That decision led to appeals from the club's players, former India captain Sunil Chhetri and AIFF president Kalyan Chaubey, all asking the Tata Group to reconsider.

APPEAL TO TATA GROUP

We, the players of Jamshedpur, with folded hands plead to Tata’s Top Leadership to rethink their decision. And not destroy the future of Indian Football. This club is the heart and soul of Indian football and the only hope for lakhs of upcoming players. pic.twitter.com/aEsmdHGxSl

— Pratik Chaudhari (@pratikch89) August 1, 2026

There is certainly a football ecosystem beyond the ISL, but the country's top division is currently dealing with questions that go well beyond how many clubs are being formed.

THE ISL PROBLEMS ARE GETTING HARD TO IGNORE

The trouble with the ISL has been building for some time.

The commercial agreement between the All India Football Federation (AIFF) and Football Sports Development Limited (FSDL), which had been central to the league's operation, expired before the previous season. The uncertainty around the commercial structure contributed to a drastically shortened 2025-26 campaign.

The season, which was initially expected to begin in September, eventually ran from February 14 to May 21 and was played in a single-leg format.

That meant fewer matches and fewer opportunities to generate revenue for clubs that were already carrying substantial operating costs.

Industry estimates suggest ISL clubs are losing around Rs 25-30 crore per season, while broadcast revenues have fallen sharply. The reported per-match valuation dropped from around Rs 1.68 crore in 2024-25 to Rs 9.5 lakh last season.

And the problems are not limited to Jamshedpur.

  • Mumbai City FC saw City Football Group divest its stake.
  • Kerala Blasters are facing financial uncertainty and are understood to be discussing a complete stake sale.
  • Hyderabad FC were acquired by the BC Jindal Group after struggling to sustain their losses and were subsequently rebranded as Sporting Club Delhi.
  • Diamond Harbour FC, newly promoted to the ISL, are also facing questions over their future.

The new club-led commercial model is meant to give teams greater control over their own revenues, sponsorships and broadcasting arrangements. That could eventually prove to be a positive change.

But asking financially stretched clubs to become their own commercial engines does not magically make the underlying problem disappear.

A NATIONAL TEAM FULL OF MESS

The uncertainty is not restricted to the club game. India's national-team setup has also offered some uncomfortable examples of how decisions are being handled.

The Ranjit Bajaj-Bibiano Fernandes episode is a good example. Bajaj was approved as manager of the India U-15 men's team after Fernandes was appointed head coach, but objected to the arrangement because he felt their footballing philosophies were too different.

He initially turned down the role and later said he was ready to take it if Fernandes was not part of the setup. What made the episode more concerning was the communication around the appointments, with Bajaj saying he had not been informed beforehand and did not receive timely confirmation even after reports about the decision emerged.

This is a team preparing for India's first appearance at the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival. Time spent debating the structure of the coaching setup is time not spent scouting, building combinations and preparing the players.

Then there is the national-team calendar itself.

The proposed Brazil friendly in October has drawn criticism from former India captain Bhaichung Bhutia because of its potential clash with India's participation in the FIFA ASEAN Cup. If the fixtures overlap, India could find itself having to choose between a high-profile friendly and a competitive international tournament.

VIDEO | On India hosting five times World Champions Brazil for a friendly game in Kolkata on October 3, 2026, All India Football Federation (AIFF) president Kalyan Chaubey said:

"The more we get international matches, international friendly... we might not win those matches but pic.twitter.com/rrZbhnjxYy

— Press Trust of India (@PTI_News) August 7, 2026

These are not signs of a football system that has everything under control.

SO, WHERE IS THE EXCELLENT PROGRESS?

Mandaviya's latest comment only widens the gap between how the Sports Ministry sees Indian football and how fans experience it.

For supporters already frustrated by the mess around the sport, "excellent progress" feels like an added insult to the injuries.

Earlier, during a crucial ISL press conference, he struggled to pronounce Mohun Bagan and East Bengal, calling them "Mohun Began" and "East Began" before seeking help.

It quickly became a meme, but for football fans, the moment went deeper than that. These are not just two ISL clubs. They are century-old institutions that are central to India's football history, particularly in Kolkata.

Now comes the "excellent progress" comment.

Mandaviya spoke at length about India's preparations for the Commonwealth Games and Asian Games, including facilities being developed to help athletes perform well. But when the conversation turned to Indian football, his answer was limited to the ISL returning and new clubs being formed.

There was no mention of Jamshedpur FC's withdrawal, the financial strain on ISL clubs, the collapse in broadcast revenues, the commercial uncertainty or even the Ranjit Bajaj-Bibiano Fernandes mess. Either these are being consciously overlooked, or the people overseeing Indian sport simply aren't aware of how bad things have become.

The ISL returning is good news. New clubs are good news too. But neither explains how Indian football, at this moment, can be described as making "excellent progress".

Maybe the Sports Ministry sees a bigger picture.

If it does, Indian football fans deserve to know what that picture looks like.

news.n_title: Monsoon clouds begin to disappear as El Nino eyes a comeback over India
news.n_description: Satellite imagery shows monsoon cloud cover retreating across large parts of India and the Bay of Bengal. The shift has revived concerns that El Nino may be steering the season into another subdued phase.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
India’s monsoon appears to be losing some of its recent strength, with satellite imagery showing a noticeable reduction in cloud cover across large parts of the country and even over the Bay of Bengal.

The changing pattern has raised fresh concerns that El Nino could be beginning to influence the Indian monsoon after weeks of relatively active rainfall.

At present, the low-pressure system (LPS) over central India remains the primary weather system generating clouds and rainfall. Its influence is largely concentrated over central parts of the country, while large areas elsewhere are beginning to see a decline in monsoon activity.

One of the more significant signals is the reduction in cloud cover over the Bay of Bengal, a key moisture source for the Indian monsoon.

A decrease in organised cloud activity over the Bay of Bengal can indicate weakening moisture transport towards the Indian landmass, potentially limiting the formation and movement of rain-bearing systems.

The monsoon axis is also shifting southwards. This change is likely to push the most active rainfall zone away from the northern plains, bringing mainly dry weather back to Delhi-NCR, Haryana, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh.

While isolated areas could still receive rain, the showers are expected to be short-lived. Moderate rainfall may occur at a few places, particularly during the afternoon and evening hours, but a widespread spell of rain is not currently expected across the region.

The emerging pattern comes at a time when scientists and weather watchers are closely tracking the development of El Nino conditions in the Pacific Ocean. El Nino is typically associated with changes in atmospheric circulation that can weaken or disrupt the Indian summer monsoon, although its influence varies from one event to another.

The latest satellite signals do not necessarily mean that the monsoon has collapsed. India continues to have active rainfall-producing systems, particularly over central India. However, the rapid reduction in cloud cover and weakening activity over the Bay of Bengal suggest that the monsoon may be entering another subdued phase.

For northern India, the immediate takeaway is a return to hotter and largely dry conditions, punctuated by occasional localised showers.

The key question now is whether the weakening cloud shield is temporary, or the first clear sign that El Nino is beginning to regain control over India’s monsoon.

news.n_title: Bengal teen stays in ponds for days, claims 'jinn' makes his body burn
news.n_description: A 16-year-old in Bengal's Murshidabad has been spending days at a time in local ponds, saying the water relieves a burning sensation. Residents are concerned about his worsening health and hope he gets proper medical treatment.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
A 16-year-old teen named Iqbal Sheikh has gone viral for 'living' in ponds in Bengal’s Murshidabad. Locals say he has spent days, sometimes nearly a week at a stretch in the water to hide from unseen forces, a jinn to be precise.

Local residents said Iqbal has been spending both days and nights in different ponds around Beldanga. Meanwhile, Iqbal claimed that he experienced an intense burning sensation across his body whenever he came out of the water. Once he got back into the pond, he said, the discomfort subsided.

Iqbal believes that an unseen force is responsible for what he experiences. He has attributed it to the presence of a jinn, fairy or other supernatural entity.

However, his unusual routine appears to be taking a physical toll.

After spending prolonged periods in the water, the skin on his hands, feet and other parts of his body had turned pale. He has also developed cold and cough symptoms, according to locals.

Iqbal says he sought treatment at a local block primary health centre but did not receive the help he needed. His family is also facing financial difficulties and, according to the account, cannot afford treatment at a private hospital.

Watch here:

As concern around the teenager has grown, so has public attention. Every day, schoolchildren and local residents reportedly gather around the ponds to watch him. Some visitors have even begun bringing him food, including chuda (flattened rice), biscuits and other snacks.

But helping him leave the water has proved difficult. Locals say repeated attempts to persuade Iqbal to return home have not worked.

His story has now become a talking point across the village, drawing both curiosity and concern. While some residents remain focused on his claims about supernatural forces, the more immediate worry is his health and the physical consequences of spending several consecutive days in water.

However, the 'jinn theory' may not be the case for Iqbal as his experience has drawn attention to a rare condition known as Aquagenic Pruritus.

It is a rare dermatological condition recognised in medical literature and international clinical databases, but it is not included in India’s official notified rare-disease list.

For now, the 16-year-old continues to spend long stretches in the ponds, while residents watch from the banks and worry about how long he can continue living this way.

(With inputs from Sabyasachi Banerjee)

news.n_title: Indian student accused of strangling US girlfriend arrested at Germany airport
news.n_description: Indian student Varun Batchigari has been arrested in Germany after allegedly strangling his 19-year-old girlfriend Julissa Rubi Salazar to death in Arizona. Police say Batchigari fled Tucson and travelled to Germany while attempting to return to India.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
A 20-year-old Indian national has been arrested in Germany after allegedly strangling his 19-year-old girlfriend in Arizona and attempting to flee the United States. According to US media reports, Varun Batchigari is suspected of first-degree murder in the death of college student Julissa Rubi Salazar, who was found dead inside her apartment near the University of Arizona in Tucson on Thursday.

Police said Salazar's family requested a welfare check after becoming concerned about her. Officers who arrived at the apartment at around 4 PM (local time) found the teenager unresponsive with signs of trauma, according to the Tucson Police Department.

Investigators subsequently identified Batchigari, Salazar's boyfriend, as the prime suspect. According to KOLD, detectives believe he took Salazar's phone and credit cards and sent several messages to her mother.

POLICE TRACE SUSPECT TO GERMANY

The search for Batchigari began after police discovered he had fled Tucson. He travelled to Tucson International Airport and boarded a flight to Houston. From there, he took another flight bound for Berlin, Germany. Authorities believe he was attempting to make his way back to India.

An arrest warrant was issued as investigators tracked his movements. The Tucson Police Department said Arizona authorities worked with federal agents to locate and detain Batchigari after he arrived in Germany. He is expected to be extradited to Arizona, where he will face a first-degree murder charge and be booked into Pima County Adult Detention.

GIRLFRIEND PLANNED TO END RELATIONSHIP

The case has also drawn attention to Batchigari's relationship with Salazar and the allegations of abuse surrounding it. According to KOLD, Salazar had been planning to end the relationship after experiencing sexual assault and abusive behaviour.

Her roommates had reportedly become concerned days before her death after hearing loud screaming coming from Salazar's room on August 5. The roommates later contacted her to check whether she was safe. They received a response saying she was fine and that the incident had only been an argument.

Investigators are also looking into allegations involving Batchigari's previous conduct. According to records cited by The New York Post, he had an open criminal case in Pima County Court involving an allegation of assault -- knowingly causing injury -- filed on May 26. One woman also reportedly told investigators that Batchigari had sexually assaulted her on Halloween, although she did not report the alleged incident at the time.

UNIVERSITY STUDENT WITH TROUBLED RECORD

Batchigari had been studying business analytics at the University of Arizona. However, his time at the university was reportedly cut short after he was expelled following a fight. He also had a history of domestic violence allegations, according to reports.

The case has raised further questions about his circumstances in the weeks before Salazar's death. Batchigari had recently lost his job, which affected his ability to pay rent and put his immigration status at risk. Authorities have not said whether those circumstances played a role in the killing or his decision to leave the United States.

news.n_title: Indian professor wins eminent Dirac Medal, joins Hawking and other physics giants
news.n_description: Professor Deepak Dhar has been awarded the 2026 Dirac Medal for contributions to statistical mechanics. The honour adds to a career that took him from UP's Pratapgarh to Caltech and back to India.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Deepak Dhar, an IINSA distinguished professor and one of India’s most respected theoretical physicists, has been awarded the 2026 Dirac Medal by the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP), a recognition considered among the highest honours in the field of physics.

The award, instituted in 1985, has over the decades been associated with some of the biggest names, including Stephen Hawkings, in theoretical physics.

Dhar is one of four physicists selected this year in recognition of their significant contributions to statistical mechanics.

HONOUR FOR WORK IN STATISTICAL MECHANICS

ICTP said the 2026 Dirac Medal recognises physicists whose work has significantly advanced the understanding of statistical mechanics, the branch of physics that studies how systems with a very large number of particles behave collectively.

The field is not limited to theoretical research. Scientists say it provides tools that are increasingly useful in understanding artificial intelligence, complex networks, and even financial markets.

Dhar has long been associated with the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences, Bengaluru, and has spent decades working on problems related to complex physical systems.

A JOURNEY THAT BEGAN IN A SMALL TOWN

Born in 1951 in Pratapgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Dhar grew up in a Hindi-medium environment. His mother hoped he would become an IAS officer, but his father encouraged a different kind of curiosity.

He once recalled that his father regularly brought home science magazines.

One magazine in particular, Understanding Science, left a lasting impression on him.

Dhar studied at Allahabad University before moving to IIT Kanpur for his MSc. He later went to the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in the United States, where he received a Richard Feynman fellowship.

At Caltech, he worked closely with the legendary physicist Richard Feynman and served as his teaching assistant. Dhar completed his PhD in 1978.

For many young scientists, such a path would naturally lead to a career in the United States. Dhar, however, chose to return to India.

RETURN TO INDIA

After finishing his doctorate, Dhar joined the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) in Mumbai. He also served as a professor at IISER Pune for almost 8 years, says his LinkedIn profile, contributing to the development in the field of Physics and taught hundreds of students.

At TIFR, he worked without a formal mentor but became part of a strong community of theoretical physicists. Over the next four decades, he made major contributions to statistical physics.

Among his best-known achievements is Dhar’s burning algorithm, developed in connection with sandpile models, which has become an influential concept in the study of self-organised criticality and complex systems.

A SERIES OF MAJOR RECOGNITIONS

The Dirac Medal is the latest in a string of international and national honours received by Dhar.

In 2022, he became the first Indian to receive the Boltzmann Medal, widely regarded as the highest honour in statistical physics.

Reflecting on that recognition, Dhar had said:

“While I am the first Indian to win the Boltzmann Medal, I am not the first Indian who has done good work in statistical physics.”

In 2023, the Government of India awarded him the Padma Bhushan, the country’s third-highest civilian honour.

The ICTP Dirac Medal is a prestigious annual award given by the International Centre for Theoretical Physics in honour of physicist Paul Dirac. Started in 1985, it recognises outstanding work in theoretical physics and mathematics.

The medal is not awarded to Nobel, Fields, or Wolf Prize winners, although several past Dirac medallists later went on to receive those honours.

For many in the scientific community, Dhar’s story carries importance beyond awards and medals.

A student who learned English through science magazines in a small town in Uttar Pradesh went on to study with one of the world’s greatest physicists, had the opportunity to build a career abroad, yet chose to return to India and contribute to Indian science.

His latest recognition from ICTP is being seen not only as a tribute to a distinguished physicist, but also as a reminder of how curiosity, persistence, and a commitment to science in India can shape achievements that earn global respect.

news.n_title: Will pure petrol come from your father's house? BJP MP jabs ethanol critics
news.n_description: BJP MP Janardan Mishra defended the Centre's ethanol-blending policy and taunted its critics over demands for pure petrol. His remarks come amid continued debate over E20 fuel, engine performance and India's dependence on imported crude.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Janardan Mishra, the BJP MP from Madhya Pradesh's Rewa, has sparked fresh controversy with a sharp defence of the Centre’s ethanol-blending policy, asking critics of the move whether “pure petrol” would come from their “father’s house”.

Backing the Centre’s push for 20 per cent ethanol blending in petrol, Mishra argued that India remains heavily dependent on imported crude oil.

He said India produces only around 20 per cent of the crude oil it needs, while the remaining 80 per cent is imported.

Referring to the prevailing geopolitical situation and challenges in transporting crude, the BJP leader said oil tankers sometimes have to travel an additional 18,000 km to bring supplies to India.

“In such a situation, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi talks about blending 20 per cent ethanol in petrol, some people start protesting,” Mishra said.

He took aim at those opposing ethanol blending, saying, “A movement is underway claiming that ethanol won't work, pure petrol will. Will pure petrol come from your father's house? If there's no pure petrol in the country, where will it come from?”

Mishra further questioned the opposition to ethanol-powered vehicles and said India needed to increase domestic production of alternative fuels.

“If ethanol is not produced, where will petrol come from, where will diesel come from?” he asked.

The Rewa MP also cited Brazil's extensive use of ethanol, claiming that vehicles there can run entirely on the fuel.He said Indian vehicles were also capable of running on ethanol-blended petrol.

“Brazil produces the maximum ethanol in the world, which is why vehicles there run on 100 per cent ethanol,” Mishra said.

He claimed that experts in India had found that ethanol blending does not damage vehicle engines and alleged that the opposition to the policy was “unnecessary”.

Mishra's comments come amid continuing debate over the government's ethanol-blending programme and its impact on vehicle performance, fuel economy and consumers.

The Centre has maintained that extensive testing and field experience with E20 petrol — containing 20 per cent ethanol — have found no evidence of abnormal engine wear, corrosion or a reduction in vehicle life.

Mishra also praised the government's broader push for alternative fuels, including biogas and CNG, and highlighted initiatives aimed at improving air connectivity.

news.n_title: Indian startup tests space tow truck to save dying satellites: What is it?
news.n_description: Aule Space has tested its relative guidance, navigation and control technology at Isro's Rendezvous Simulation Laboratory, reaching TRL-6. The milestone strengthens India's private push into orbital servicing for failed satellites and debris management.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
In a development that could mark a shift in how India approaches the growing problem of space debris and satellite failures, Bengaluru-based deep-tech startup Aule Space has successfully tested its relative guidance, navigation and control (GNC) technology at ISRO’s Rendezvous Simulation Laboratory (RSL), achieving Technology Readiness Level 6 (TRL-6).

Aule Space says it is the first private company to access and test its technology at the facility, where its autonomous navigation system was evaluated in simulated space environments.

The technology addresses one of the most difficult challenges in the emerging orbital economy: rendezvous, proximity operations and docking (RPOD).

We have successfully tested our relative guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) stack at ISRO’s Rendezvous Simulation Laboratory (RSL), achieving TRL 6. We are the first private company to access and test at this facility. pic.twitter.com/kgkzUf4gMa

— Aule Space (@AuleSpace) August 8, 2026

WHAT IS TOW TRUCK FOR SPACE?

Hundreds of active satellites currently operate in Low Earth Orbit, travelling at speeds of nearly 28,000 kmph.

Many are worth hundreds of millions of dollars and provide critical services ranging from communications and navigation to agriculture, defence and Earth observation.

But satellites can become unusable because of something as simple as depleted propellant, a failed thruster or a mechanical malfunction. Once a spacecraft becomes non-responsive, servicing it is extremely difficult—particularly if it was never designed to be refuelled or docked with another spacecraft.

pic.twitter.com/Cjkwp9Rf6e

— Aule Space (@AuleSpace) May 12, 2025

Aule Space, founded by Jay Panchal, Nithyaa Giri and Hrishit Tambi, is attempting to solve this problem by developing autonomous spacecraft that could effectively function as “tow trucks” for satellites.

The company's servicing spacecraft are designed to approach and interact with non-cooperative targets, including satellites that may be tumbling or unable to communicate.

Using computer vision and autonomous navigation, the spacecraft would have to determine the target's position, velocity and rotation before safely approaching it.

The challenge is comparable to trying to dock with a car travelling at nearly 28,000 kmph, while operating in darkness and without conventional GPS, and with the target potentially spinning uncontrollably.

Once attached, a servicing spacecraft could potentially provide propulsion to a satellite, help maintain its orbit or move a failed spacecraft away from operational orbital lanes.

BIG PLANS AHEAD

Aule Space has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding to support hardware development and eventual orbital validation of its technology.

The successful TRL-6 demonstration is an important step towards that goal.

If such systems eventually reach orbit, they could help extend the operational life of expensive satellites, reduce the creation of new debris and enable a future in which spacecraft are not simply abandoned after they fail.

For India, the technology also signals an expansion of the country's private space ambitions, from building and launching spacecraft to servicing and maintaining them once they reach orbit.

news.n_title: 17-year-old from Tamil Nadu wins Rs 3.55 crore scholarship to Brown University
news.n_description: Pranav Ilango from Tamil Nadu's Erode is set to study at Brown University in the US after securing a full scholarship worth Rs 3.55 crore. The scholarship covers his tuition and living expenses throughout his four-year undergraduate programme at the Ivy League university.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
At 17, Pranav Ilango is taking a dream that began in Erode, Tamil Nadu, to the halls of Brown University, one of the world’s most prestigious institutions located in Rhode Island, US.

Pranav has secured admission to Brown with a full scholarship valued at Rs 3.55 crore, covering his tuition and living expenses for all four years. He will study Public Health and Applied Mathematics, bringing together mathematics, technology and data to understand complex problems, develop solutions and improve lives.

Besides Brown, he also secured a 100% scholarship offer from The University of Hong Kong, underscoring the global recognition of his academic achievements.

Behind Pranav's Ivy League admission is a journey that goes far beyond academic achievement. For Pranav, this moment represents years of learning, preparation, mentorship and a growing desire to use education for something larger than himself.

His long-term goal is to bring together technology, mathematics, and public health to tackle real-world problems, especially those impacting underserved communities.

From a dream nurtured in Erode to a new chapter at Brown, Pranav’s journey is a reminder that ambition can begin anywhere, and that true success lies not only in what one achieves, but in the impact one hopes to create.

FROM ERODE TO THE IVY LEAGUE

A senior student at CS Academy, Erode, Pranav began preparing for his international academic journey at an early age.

At just 13, he joined Dexterity Global’s National Scholar Development Programme. Over the years, the mentorship and training he received through the programme helped him develop not only academically, but also as a leader and problem-solver. It encouraged him to approach learning with curiosity, discipline and a broader sense of purpose.

His academic journey has been marked by exceptional achievements. He was recognised among the Outstanding Cambridge Learners, including a World Topper distinction in IGCSE Mathematics, placing him among a select group of high-achieving students.

But mathematics, for Pranav, is not simply a subject to excel in. It is a tool for understanding problems and finding ways to solve them.

MATHEMATICS WITH A PURPOSE

Pranav has developed a strong interest in software, entrepreneurship, engineering and data-driven problem-solving. His interests have increasingly converged around a larger question: how can technology and data be used to improve people's lives?

His long-term goal is to build a public-health venture that can provide meaningful data insights to governments and communities, particularly in underserved regions where access to reliable information and resources can be limited.

He has also explored technology-driven solutions in education and healthcare, including work involving artificial intelligence, programming and data science.

This makes his choice of Public Health and Applied Mathematics at Brown particularly significant. Rather than viewing these as separate fields, Pranav sees an opportunity to bring them together, using mathematical thinking, technology and data to better understand public-health challenges and develop practical solutions.

For him, mathematics has a purpose beyond numbers. It can become a means of understanding communities, identifying patterns and helping decision-makers respond to problems that affect millions of people.

A LIFE-CHANGING OPPORTUNITY

Founded in 1764, Brown is one of the eight Ivy League universities and among the most selective institutions in the United States. Its academic environment, interdisciplinary approach and strengths across mathematics, science and the humanities offer Pranav an opportunity to explore the intersection of the fields that have shaped his ambitions.

For Pranav, however, getting to Brown is only the beginning.

He believes that the mentorship and training he has received over the years have shaped not only how he learns, but also how he thinks, solves problems and leads. At Brown, he hopes to deepen his understanding of mathematics, technology and public health, and use that knowledge to create meaningful solutions for India.

A JOURNEY THAT IS JUST BEGINNING

Pranav’s story is remarkable not simply because of the Rs 3.55-crore scholarship or the name of the university on his admission letter.

It is the story of a young student from Erode who began thinking about a future beyond geographical boundaries at an early age, and then worked consistently to turn that ambition into reality.

His journey also highlights the importance of mentorship. From his early years of preparation to his academic achievements and now his admission to Brown, Pranav’s path has been shaped by learning, guidance and a willingness to think beyond conventional boundaries.

His next chapter will take him from Tamil Nadu to one of the world’s leading universities. But the larger ambition remains rooted in the purpose that has guided him so far: using knowledge, technology and data to solve meaningful problems and create opportunities for communities that need them most.

From a classroom in Erode to the Ivy League, Pranav Ilango’s journey is a powerful reminder that talent can emerge from anywhere. With the right guidance, determination and purpose, even the biggest dreams can find a way forward.

news.n_title: 62% investors follow finfluencers. Sebi is using AI to hunt down fake tips and fraud
news.n_description: Sebi has deployed Project SUDARSAN to track misleading investment content and finfluencer activity on social media. The move comes as its investor survey shows how widely such content shapes investing decisions and fraud risks.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Sebi is turning to artificial intelligence to keep a closer watch on financial influencers and fraudulent investment content on social media, as its latest investor survey shows that a large majority of investors are influenced by finfluencers.

The market regulator has operationalised Project SUDARSAN, an AI-powered surveillance platform designed to monitor unauthorised digital activity and detect content that could mislead investors.

Sebi's latest Investor Survey found that 62% of investors are influenced by finfluencers. The regulator has flagged the lack of accountability and verified performance data among many such influencers as a concern, particularly when investors rely on their content to make financial decisions.

HOW SEBI IS USING AI TO WATCH FINFLUENCERS

Project SUDARSAN, which stands for Surveillance of Unauthorised Digital Activity via Real-time Scanner for Anti-fraud, is an AI-powered intelligence platform that Sebi has developed to move from conventional monitoring to more proactive surveillance.

The system uses what Sebi describes as advanced multimodal AI. That means it can analyse different forms of information at the same time, including spoken language, visual cues and contextual intent. It can also analyse content in regional languages.

The system combines these signals with behavioural and regulatory parameters and assigns risk scores to the content it identifies. It then generates structured alerts that can be examined for possible regulatory action.

This is significant because financial fraud on social media does not always appear as a straightforward written recommendation. A video, an image, an advertisement or a message can all be used to make claims about investments.

SUDARSAN is therefore designed to continuously scan public content across major social media platforms, including videos, messages, images and advertisements.

Sebi says the system has specifically been engineered to identify deceptive practices such as guaranteed-return claims, fraudulent certifications, impersonation of regulated entities and the provision of unregistered investment advice.

FROM GUARANTEED RETURNS TO FAKE CERTIFICATIONS

One of the biggest risks for retail investors is that financial content on social media can look credible even when the person behind it is not authorised to provide investment advice.

A post promising guaranteed returns, for example, can be presented as an investment opportunity rather than an obvious scam. Similarly, someone can use fake credentials or impersonate a regulated entity to create the impression that the advice or investment product is legitimate.

SUDARSAN is designed to look for precisely these kinds of signals.

The system does not only search for particular words. Sebi says it analyses spoken language, visual cues and contextual intent, while also using behavioural and regulatory parameters to generate risk scores. This allows the regulator to move towards automated identification of potentially suspicious content rather than depending entirely on manual monitoring.

SEBI HAS ALREADY FLAGGED MORE THAN 20,000 INSTANCES

The scale of the monitoring is already significant.

Sebi said that since Project SUDARSAN began in November 2025, it has identified more than 20,000 instances of fraudulent content and posts across social media.

The regulator said the system has also helped reduce the burden of manual oversight while strengthening its ability to monitor digital activity that could undermine market integrity.

The number is particularly significant when viewed against the rapid expansion of retail participation in the securities market and the growing role of social media in how investors discover financial information.

SEBI IS ALSO TRYING TO STOP UNAUTHORISED ADS

SUDARSAN is not Sebi's only technology-based intervention.

The regulator has also implemented an API-based framework in collaboration with social media platform providers so that advertisements related to the securities market can be run only by verified, Sebi-registered intermediaries.

This creates another layer of screening. While SUDARSAN focuses on identifying suspicious public content, the advertising framework is aimed at preventing unauthorised entities from using social media platforms to promote securities-market related advertisements in the first place.

Sebi has also deployed R(AI)DAR, an AI-powered monitoring and enforcement support tool for asset management companies. The system reviews advertisements and investor education material and can identify compliance issues, including products being promoted in the guise of educational content and missing mandatory disclaimers.

Together, these systems show how Sebi is increasingly using technology not just after a complaint is received, but to identify potentially problematic content before it reaches or misleads more investors.

WHY SEBI IS WORRIED ABOUT FINFLUENCERS

The concern is not simply that people are consuming financial content on social media.

The bigger issue is what happens when investors treat that content as investment advice without knowing whether the person giving it is regulated, whether the performance claims can be verified or whether the risks have been properly disclosed.

Sebi's own report points to this information gap. It says the 62% finding on finfluencer influence highlights the risks posed by people operating without accountability or verified performance data.

The regulator is therefore building multiple layers of protection around the investor.

Alongside surveillance, Sebi has introduced the Sebi Check facility and validated UPI handles to help investors verify whether they are making payments to genuine Sebi-registered intermediaries. It has also partnered with Google Play on a verified app label initiative aimed at helping investors identify legitimate stock-trading apps.

The idea is to make it harder for an investor to be misled at different points — from discovering an investment idea on social media to downloading an app and finally transferring money.

BIGGER PROBLEM IS THAT PEOPLE ARE LISTENING

The 62% figure becomes more important when viewed alongside Sebi's wider Investor Survey.

The survey covered more than 90,000 households across urban and rural India and examined how people move from awareness of securities products to actual participation.

It found that 63% of Indian households, or approximately 213 million households, are aware of at least one securities product, including mutual funds, shares and bonds. But only 9.5%, or around 32.1 million households, actually invest in these markets.

That means there is a large pool of Indians who know that these investment products exist but have not yet started investing.

The survey found that 74% of non-investors cite the complexity of products and a lack of understanding as barriers. Another 73% are concerned about potential losses, while 51% have low trust in financial institutions and transparency.

This creates a natural opening for social media creators. People who find traditional financial products difficult to understand may turn to short videos, social media posts and influencers for simpler explanations.

Sebi's survey found that 80% of respondents preferred short-form videos as a way of learning, while 69% preferred social media. Regional languages were also in strong demand, with 47% preferring regional-language content and another 47% preferring Hindi.

That makes the influence of finfluencers a much bigger issue than just social-media chatter. For a large number of potential investors, these platforms are becoming part of the route through which they learn about investing.

And Sebi's challenge is to ensure that the information reaching those investors is not only easy to understand, but also accurate, transparent and legally compliant.

news.n_title: 73-year-old filmmaker Shakeel Noorani arrested on rape, sexual assault charges
news.n_description: Filmmaker Shakeel Noorani has been arrested after a 33-year-old actor accused him of rape, sexual assault and blackmail. Police say he was traced to Satara after weeks of evading arrest and remains in custody as the investigation continues.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Filmmaker Shakeel Noorani was arrested by Mumbai Police on Saturday in connection with a rape, sexual assault and blackmail case filed by a 33-year-old actor. The 73-year-old filmmaker was arrested from a farmhouse in Maharashtra's Satara district after allegedly evading arrest for around 40 days.

Noorani was arrested by the Malwani police and is currently in police custody. A case has been registered against him under relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. His lawyer, however, has denied the allegations against him.

According to the police complaint, the actor first came in contact with Noorani in 2016 and alleged that he sexually exploited her repeatedly over the years. She further alleged that Noorani drugged her and recorded videos of her in compromising situations.

She also alleged that Noorani blackmailed her by threatening to make the videos public. According to her complaint, she suffered a miscarriage as a result of the alleged incidents.

Following the complaint, the police registered a case and launched an investigation to trace Noorani. He was subsequently arrested from a farmhouse in Satara district after allegedly remaining untraceable for around 40 days.

Deputy Commissioner of Police Sandeep Ghuge confirmed Noorani's arrest. "We have arrested him and we are investigating this case as per law," he said.

Noorani has been associated with Bollywood films including Bade Dilwala (1999) and Joru Ka Ghulam (2000).

The investigation is currently underway, and the allegations against Noorani are yet to be established in court.

news.n_title: Meet CSIR scientist Akanksha Singh who completed a rare hat-trick of science honours
news.n_description: CSIR-CIMAP scientist Dr Akanksha Singh has been selected for the NASI Young Scientist Award 2026, completing a rare hat-trick of national recognitions in a single year. Here's what her research in crop protection and agricultural science focuses on, and why it matters for India's farmers.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
For most researchers, earning one national recognition is a career milestone. For Dr Akanksha Singh, 2026 has brought three.

The Scientist-D at the CSIR-Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants has now been selected for the National Academy of Sciences, India (NASI) Young Scientist Award 2026 in the field of Agricultural and Plant Sciences, completing a remarkable hat-trick of prestigious honours in a single year.

Earlier in 2026, she was inducted as an Indian National Young Academy of Sciences (INYAS) Member and selected as an Indian National Science Academy (INSA) Young Associate, making her one of the few young researchers to receive all three national recognitions in the same year.

According to CSIR-CIMAP, the achievement reflects her growing contribution to agricultural science and sustainable crop research.

THE SCIENCE BEHIND HER RESEARCH

Dr Singh holds a PhD in Botany and currently serves as Scientist-D in the Division of Crop Protection and Production at CSIR-CIMAP.

Her research goes far beyond conventional crop protection. According to her research profile, she studies plant-microbe interactions, biological crop protection, fungal diseases, eco-friendly disease management, fungicide development and sustainable agriculture.

In simple terms, her work explores how beneficial microbes can naturally protect crops from harmful fungal diseases, reducing dependence on chemical pesticides while improving crop productivity. The research also aims to strengthen plant health through environmentally friendly farming practices.

For a country where millions depend on agriculture, such innovations could help farmers protect crops while making cultivation more sustainable.

A RISING NAME IN INDIAN SCIENCE

CSIR-CIMAP is one of India's premier research institutes dedicated to medicinal and aromatic plants, with scientists working on agriculture, biotechnology and natural products.

Dr Singh has steadily built her career in agricultural science, and the three national honours this year mark growing recognition of her work within India's scientific community.

She is among 16 scientists selected for the NASI Young Scientist Award 2026 across multiple disciplines.

WHAT IS THE NASI YOUNG SCIENTIST AWARD?

Founded in 1930, the National Academy of Sciences, India is one of India's oldest scientific academies.

Its Young Scientist Award recognises early-career researchers who have made outstanding scientific contributions and encourages them to pursue high-impact research.

Dr Singh will receive the award during the 96th Annual Session and Symposium of NASI, scheduled to be held at Banaras Hindu University on December 4 and 5, 2026.

The honour also shines a spotlight on a new generation of Indian scientists developing practical solutions to some of agriculture's biggest challenges, from crop diseases to sustainable food production.

news.n_title: Rural jobs under new VB-G RAM G scheme fall nearly 50% in first month
news.n_description: Official data showed person-days under VB-G RAM G fell to 7.67 crore in July from 15.33 crore a year earlier. The sharp drop in the scheme's first full month has raised fresh questions over implementation and rural job generation.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Employment generation under the government's newly launched rural jobs programme nearly halved in its first month, with person-days generated falling to 7.67 crore in July from 15.33 crore in the same month last year, according to official data.

The 49.94% year-on-year decline comes just weeks after the Centre replaced the two-decade-old Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) with the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin), or VB-G RAM G, from July 1.

A person-day refers to one person being provided employment for one day under the programme and is the standard measure used to track work generated under the rural jobs scheme.

The government has projected VB-G RAM G as an upgraded version of MGNREGS, increasing the annual employment guarantee from 100 days to 125 days while also raising wages. The revamped programme also aims to place greater emphasis on durable rural asset creation and improving livelihoods.

The Ministry of Rural Development has maintained that the transition to the new programme has not affected implementation.

In a written reply in Parliament last month, the government said more than 99.5% of workers demanding employment under VB-G RAM G had been provided work, with over 5.2 crore person-days generated by July 22.

The latest month-end figures, however, indicate employment generation slowed further through the remainder of July.

The government has not yet issued a detailed explanation for the nearly 50% year-on-year decline in person-days generated during the first full month of the scheme.

The July data marks the first full-month performance of VB-G RAM G since its rollout. The employment figures in the coming months are expected to indicate whether the sharp decline was linked to the transition from MGNREGS or reflects a broader slowdown in rural job generation.

The government launched VB-G RAM G with a higher annual outlay of Rs 1.52 lakh crore for 2025-26, compared with the Rs 86,000 crore budgeted for MGNREGS, while promising enhanced wages, an expanded employment guarantee and a stronger focus on creating productive rural assets.

Despite these changes, the first month's data has put the spotlight on the scheme's implementation and employment generation.

news.n_title: Can you eat food after its 'best before' date? Know the difference
news.n_description: A recent food-safety inspection in Bengaluru found rotten meat, expired dairy products, fungus-infested food and large quantities of sauces at several eateries. The case raises an important question: can food still be eaten after its best-before date?

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
A recent food-safety inspection in Bengaluru found 132 kg of food items and 15 litres of used cooking oil being seized from food businesses, with officials flagging rotten meat, expired dairy products, fungus-infested food and improperly stored preparations.

The findings have also brought attention to a common confusion among consumers: what exactly does a "best before" date mean, and is food safe to eat after it?

This distinction becomes particularly important with products such as milk, curd, packaged snacks, sauces and other foods that may remain in kitchens or refrigerators for days.

Also read: 45-kg rotten meat, expired milk: Posh Bengaluru pub shut after food safety raid

WHAT DOES 'BEST BEFORE' MEAN?

The "best before" date generally refers to the period during which a food is expected to retain its best quality, including its taste, texture and aroma, when stored as recommended.

Unlike an expiry or use-by date, food does not necessarily become unsafe the moment the best-before date passes. However, that does not mean every product is safe to consume afterwards.

This distinction is particularly important because storage conditions, the type of food and whether the package has been opened can all affect food safety.

A product may not suddenly become unsafe immediately after the best-before date. However, its quality can deteriorate over time.

This does not mean that every food item is automatically safe to consume after this date. The type of food, storage conditions, packaging and whether it has been opened all matter.

WHAT DOES 'EXPIRY DATE' MEAN?

An expiry date is different. For foods where a use-by or expiry date is relevant to safety, consuming the product after that date can carry a higher risk.

Consumers should therefore avoid treating "best before" and "expiry" as interchangeable terms.

CAN YOU EAT FOOD AFTER THE BEST-BEFORE DATE?

In some cases, a food may still be consumable after its best-before date if it has been stored properly, remains unopened and shows no signs of spoilage.

However, the date should not be considered the only factor. Foods that require refrigeration need particular care, as improper storage can allow harmful bacteria to multiply even before the printed date.

WHAT ABOUT MILK, CURD AND OTHER PERISHABLE FOODS?

Extra caution is needed with foods such as milk, curd, fresh meat, fish and other highly perishable products.

These foods can deteriorate quickly if they are not kept at the correct temperature. If the packaging is swollen, leaking or damaged, or the food has an unusual smell, colour or texture, it should not be consumed.

DON'T RELY ONLY ON SMELL

A common mistake is assuming that food is safe because it smells normal.

Some harmful microorganisms may not produce an obvious change in smell, taste or appearance. Never taste food simply to determine whether it has gone bad.

If a perishable food has been stored incorrectly or left at room temperature for too long, the printed date alone cannot guarantee its safety.

CHECK HOW THE FOOD WAS STORED

Storage instructions are just as important as the date printed on the package.

Keep refrigerated foods at the recommended temperature and follow instructions such as "refrigerate after opening". Once a product is opened, its usable life may also change depending on the food and storage conditions.

WHAT SHOULD YOU DO AFTER THE DATE?

Before consuming a food item past its best-before date, check:

  • Whether the package is damaged or swollen

  • Whether it has been opened

  • Whether it was stored according to the instructions

  • Whether there are visible signs of spoilage

  • Whether its texture, colour or appearance has changed

  • Whether it is a highly perishable food

  • When in doubt, particularly with meat, dairy and other perishable foods, it is safer to discard the product.

"Best before" does not automatically mean "unsafe after this date", while an expiry or use-by date should be taken much more seriously. The type of food, storage conditions, packaging and signs of spoilage all need to be considered.

Reading the date label correctly can help reduce both unnecessary food waste and the risk of consuming unsafe food.

news.n_title: Typhoon Dolphin is strangling India's monsoon rain from 4,000 km away
news.n_description: Typhoon Dolphin's impact is being tracked beyond China as Pacific disturbances reshape India's monsoon conditions. The focus is now on whether the Bay of Bengal sees a fresh low-pressure system or continued suppression.

n_offline_data.no_desc_withouthtml:
Typhoon Dolphin has slammed into eastern China, unleashing torrential rain and powerful winds, but nearly 4,000 kilometres away, India is facing a very different consequence of an increasingly active Pacific, a weakening monsoon.

Dolphin, the most powerful tropical cyclone to hit China so far this year, made landfall near Yuhuan in Zhejiang province on August 9 with sustained winds of around 151 kmph.

More than a million people were evacuated as the storm brought widespread flooding risks across eastern China.

But the bigger story for India lies not in Dolphin's rainfall, but in the highly disturbed atmospheric conditions across the Pacific Ocean.

HOW IS TYPHOON DOLPHIN STRANGLING INDIAN MONSOON RAIN?

Satellite imagery shows a hyperactive Pacific, with multiple weather systems developing across the tropical and western Pacific. Such intense activity can influence the large-scale atmospheric circulation that connects the Pacific with the Indian monsoon region.

This is where the El Nino connection becomes important.

During El Nino-type conditions, the distribution of tropical convection and rising air shifts eastward towards the Pacific. This can alter the Walker circulation and atmospheric waves reaching the Indian Ocean, potentially suppressing convection and weakening the mechanisms that generate India's rain-bearing systems.

Research has established a strong relationship between Pacific convection, atmospheric circulation and Indian monsoon variability.

The result could be particularly significant for the Bay of Bengal, the breeding ground for many of India's monsoon low-pressure systems.

Interestingly, the Pacific does not always suppress the Indian monsoon directly. In fact, disturbances from the western North Pacific can travel westward and help trigger low-pressure systems over the Bay of Bengal.

Research shows that more than one-third of monsoon low-pressure systems can originate through downstream amplification of Pacific disturbances, with some tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific providing the atmospheric trigger.

That makes the current situation complicated.

PACIFIC OCEAN ON OVERDRIVE

A hyperactive Pacific can sometimes send disturbances towards the Bay of Bengal and revive India's monsoon.

But under an unfavourable El Nino-like background circulation, the same Pacific activity can coincide with suppressed convection over the Indian monsoon domain.

For India, the warning signs are already visible. Monsoon cloud cover has reduced across large areas, including over the Bay of Bengal, while fewer organised rain-bearing systems are developing over the country.

The monsoon is therefore not disappearing because Typhoon Dolphin directly “stole” India's rain. Instead, Dolphin is one part of a much larger atmospheric picture unfolding across the Pacific.

The key question now is whether the Pacific disturbances will eventually generate a new low-pressure system over the Bay of Bengal, or whether the El Nino-like circulation will continue to choke India's monsoon engine.
